Batch tool for dispatch

Paste one stop per line, as coordinates (49.8917, 10.8864) or as a TerrA iD. Stops are converted at the precision chosen above, grouped by area code and sorted along the grid, so neighbouring stops end up next to each other. This is a sorting aid, not an optimised route.

How a TerrA iD is built

A TerrA iD starts with a 5-character area code, about 5 km across and about as long as a postcode like 96052. A local part narrows it to a street (about 150 m), a building (about 5 m) or a doorstep (about 1 m), and a final character checks for typos. Codes that start the same sit next to each other, so parcels can be sorted, split into delivery-station zones and batched by prefix.

Postcode-style areaThe first 5 characters work as a zone for sorting and station assignment
Pick your precisionArea, street, building or doorstep, from one code family
Works offlineOpen algorithm, calculated on the device, no registration

What this prototype does not settle yet

Grid cells are squares and ignore municipal and postcode boundaries, so two neighbouring houses can fall into different area codes, and a delivery system should also check adjacent areas. Mapping an existing postcode such as 96052 to TerrA iD areas needs an official boundary database and adoption by postal operators; this page does not include one. A phone's GPS is usually accurate to a few metres, so building level is the practical default. A code marks a spot, not a recipient: flats and units still need a floor or unit number.

TerrA iD is an independent open-standard concept; the name and example codes are provisional. Earth imagery: NASA Blue Marble, via three-globe (MIT).
